pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 📐 **Strand 3 — Geometry And Measurement**
Shape, space, measurement, position and movement — the mathematics of the world around us.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B7.3.2)
- B7.3.2.3 — Demonstrate understanding of bearings, vectors and their components using real-life cases.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- describe the bearing of one point from another using three-figure bearings
- find back bearings
- distinguish between scalar and vector quantities
- draw vectors given their magnitude and bearing, and recognise the zero vector
- write vectors in column (component) form and convert between column form and magnitude–bearing form

pages.title: Bearings
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Describe the bearing of a point from another point.
Curriculum indicator B7.3.2.3.1
> 🔑 **Key idea: True bearing** — The **true bearing** of a point B from a point A is the angle measured **clockwise from the North** direction at A to the line AB. It is always written with **three figures**, from 000° to 360°, e.g. 060°, 135°, 245°.
[[fig:m7-f57|Figure 11.1: Bearings of B from A measured clockwise from North]]
## ✏️ Example 11.1
Use the diagrams above to state the bearing of B from A in each case.
**Solution**
a) **060°** b) **135°** c) 180° + 60° = **240°** d) 360° − 45° = **315°**
Note how we write 060°, not 60°: a bearing always has three digits.
> 🎯 **BECE tip** Draw a North line at the point you are measuring **from**. "The bearing of B **from** A" means the North line is at A.

pages.title: Back bearings
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Explain how to find the back bearing when the direction of travel has a bearing which is less than 180° and/or greater than 180°.
Curriculum indicator B7.3.2.3.2
> 🔑 **Key idea: Back bearing** — If the bearing of P from Q is θ, then the bearing of Q from P (the **back bearing**) is: **θ + 180°** if θ < 180°, or **θ − 180°** if θ ≥ 180°. The North lines at P and Q are parallel, so the two bearings differ by 180°.
[[fig:m7-f58|Figure 11.2: Bearing of P from Q is 060°; bearing of Q from P is 240°]]
## ✏️ Example 11.2
a) The bearing of P from Q is 060°. What is the bearing of Q from P? b) The bearing of P from Q is 145°. What is the bearing of Q from P? c) The bearing of X from Y is 290°. Find the bearing of Y from X.
**Solution**
a) 060° < 180°, so back bearing = 060° + 180° = **240°**
b) 145° + 180° = **325°**
c) 290° > 180°, so back bearing = 290° − 180° = **110°**

pages.title: Scalars and vectors
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Distinguish between scalar and vector quantities.
Curriculum indicator B7.3.2.3.3
> 🔑 **Key idea: Scalars and vectors** — A **scalar** quantity has **size (magnitude) only**, e.g. 50 kg, 3 hours. A **vector** quantity has **both magnitude and direction**, e.g. 6 km on a bearing of 245°, a force of 20 N pulling downwards.
## ✏️ Example 11.3
Group these quantities into scalars and vectors: weight, force, velocity, time, speed, distance, mass, volume, energy, work, momentum, displacement.
**Solution**
| **Scalar quantities** | **Vector quantities** |
|---|---|
| time, speed, distance, mass, volume, energy, work | weight, force, velocity, momentum, displacement |
Weight is a vector because it is the force of gravity pulling **downwards**. Speed (e.g. 60 km/h) is a scalar, but velocity (60 km/h due north) is a vector.
## Representing vectors
A vector is drawn as a directed line segment: its **length** shows the magnitude and its **arrow** shows the direction. A vector from T to R is written vec{TR} (or **TR** in bold, or as a single small letter such as **a**). It can be described in **magnitude–bearing form** as (magnitude, bearing), e.g. vec{TR} = (6 km, 245°).
## ✏️ Example 11.4
Draw the vector vec{TR} = (6 km, 245°) using a scale of 1 cm to 1 km.
**Solution**
[[fig:m7-f59]]
Figure 11.3: vec{TR} = (6 km, 245°)
1. Mark T and draw a North line at T.
2. Measure 245° clockwise from North (that is 65° past South towards West).
3. Draw a line 6 cm long in that direction and put an arrow at R.
The **magnitude** of vec{TR} is 6 km and its **bearing** is 245°.

pages.title: Keep going
pages.body: > 🔑 **Key idea: Zero vector** — The **zero vector** has magnitude 0 and no particular direction. It is just a point: e.g. walking 3 km east and then 3 km west brings you back to where you started — your displacement is the zero vector.

pages.title: Exercise 11.3
pages.body:

1. Classify as scalar or vector: a) 25 km/h b) 25 km/h on a bearing of 090° c) 60 kg d) a 10 N push to the left e) 2 hours f) 400 m south
2. Draw to scale (1 cm : 1 km): a) vec{AB} = (3 km, 060°) b) vec{QR} = (5 km, 120°) c) vec{PS} = (4 km, 300°)
3. A boy walks 4 km on a bearing of 045° and then walks 4 km back on a bearing of 225°. What is his final displacement?

parts.q: (d) a 10 N push to the left

questions.q: A boy walks 4 km on a bearing of 045° and then walks 4 km back on a bearing of 225°. What is his final displacement?

parts.a: The zero vector (he is back where he started)

pages.title: Column vectors
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Represent vectors in the column (component) form col{x;y} and determine magnitude and direction.
Curriculum indicator B7.3.2.3.4
> 🔑 **Key idea: Column vector** — On a grid, a vector can be described by how far it moves **across** (x) and how far **up or down** (y): col{x;y}. Positive x is to the right (East), negative x to the left (West); positive y is up (North), negative y is down (South). x and y are the **components** of the vector.
[[fig:m7-f60|Figure 11.4: Column vectors on a grid]]
## ✏️ Example 11.5
Write the vectors in the grid as column vectors.
**Solution**
vec{AB} = col{4;3} (4 right, 3 up); vec{CD} = col{−3;4} (3 left, 4 up); vec{EF} = col{2;−3} (2 right, 3 down); vec{GH} = col{−4;0} (4 left).
## ✏️ Example 11.6
Express graphically a) vec{PQ} = col{−3;4} b) vec{BC} = col{2;3}, and measure the bearing of each.
**Solution**
Draw each vector from a point on squared paper (see vec{CD} above for col{−3;4}).
a) col{−3;4} points up and to the left; measured clockwise from North its bearing is about **323°**.
b) col{2;3} points up and to the right; its bearing is about **034°**.
## ✏️ Example 11.7
Write as column vectors: a) (70 km, 090°) b) (10 km, 270°) c) (5 km, 030°) using a scale drawing.
**Solution**
a) 090° is due East, so all the movement is to the right: col{70;0}
b) 270° is due West: col{−10;0}
c) Draw vec{AB} 5 cm long on a bearing of 030° on graph paper (1 cm : 1 km). Read off the horizontal and vertical distances from A to B: about col{2.5;4.3}.

pages.title: Keep going
pages.body: > ✏️ **Practice:** Exercise 11.4, at the end of section 11.5, covers this section too. Tap **Quick check** to try its questions.

pages.title: Converting between column form and magnitude–bearing form
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Convert vectors in the column (component) form col{x;y} to the magnitude–bearing form (k, θ) and vice versa.
Curriculum indicator B7.3.2.3.5
The components x and y and the vector itself form a **right-angled triangle**. The magnitude of the vector is the length of the longest side (the hypotenuse), which can be found with **Pythagoras' theorem**:
> 🔑 **Key idea: Magnitude of a vector** — For vec{AB} = col{x;y}, the magnitude is $
## ✏️ Example 11.8
Find the magnitude and bearing of a) vec{AB} = col{3;4} b) vec{PQ} = col{12;5}
**Solution**
[[fig:m7-f61]]
Figure 11.5: Magnitude and direction of a column vector
a) |vec{AB}| = sqrt{3^{2} + 4^{2}} = sqrt{9 + 16} = sqrt{25} = **5 units**. Drawing the vector and measuring with a protractor, the angle from North is about 37°, so the bearing is **037°**. In magnitude–bearing form: vec{AB} ≈ (5, 037°).
b) |vec{PQ}| = sqrt{144 + 25} = sqrt{169} = **13 units**; measured bearing ≈ **067°**. So vec{PQ} ≈ (13, 067°).
## ✏️ Example 11.9
Write (25 km, 150°) as a column vector using a scale drawing.
**Solution**
Draw the vector 5 cm long (1 cm : 5 km) on a bearing of 150° (30° east of South). Measure the components: about 2.5 cm east and 4.3 cm south, i.e. about 12.5 km and 21.7 km.
(25 km, 150°) ≈ col{12.5;−21.7} km
> ✨ **Did you know?** In Basic 8 you will study Pythagoras' theorem in detail, and in senior high school you will use trigonometry to convert between these forms exactly. For now, careful scale drawing gives good answers.

pages.title: Chapter 11 summary
pages.body:
- A bearing is measured clockwise from North and written with three figures.
- Back bearing = bearing ± 180°.
- Scalars have magnitude only; vectors have magnitude and direction.
- Column vector col{x;y}: x across (right +), y up (+). Magnitude = sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}.

questions.q: The bearing of a church from a school is 248°. Find the bearing of the school from the church. ___
A plane flies on a bearing of 315°. What compass direction is this?
Is "a temperature of 30 °C" a scalar or a vector? Explain.

parts.a: Scalar — it has size only, no direction.
